submission.natural_language_explanation: L16/N3086+ is the positive half of a career/study-path axis and behaves as a graded dial: it reads positive (0.1-0.4 of scale, up to ~2x scale on institutional web text) on characterising prose about kinds and things - what something is, is made of, does or is used for - and on impersonal institutional/technical description ('Molecular biology is the study of living cells', 'A hammer is a tool used to drive nails', 'international science projects', 'The government published new rules', 'The algorithm runs in O(n log n) time'), with the peak on the sentence's salient content noun or on its closing period. It stays at the floor or below zero across a whole prompt when the content is a person's education, degree, major, training programme or career path ('She plans to study medicine next year', 'Students can choose between two majors', 'Molecular biology is the career for young students', 'He was inspired to pursue a career'), and on terse report-style sentences that only announce, schedule or quote an event ('The ministry announced...', 'The museum is open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.', 'Officials said on Thursday...'); the pole's positive activations split between a small double-negative (g-u-) component on ordinary expository tokens and a sharper gate-positive (g+u+) component on institutional/technical vocabulary, while its output direction suppresses exactly the career/specialize/pursue/choose/direction/path vocabulary that silences the pole.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The Department of Public Works operates the municipal water system under a permit issued by the state environmental agency, and it publishes an annual report on water quality. Water is drawn from two sources: a surface reservoir in the northern hills and a group of groundwater wells along the river plain. The reservoir holds roughly four billion litres when full, and its level is transmitted to the control room every fifteen minutes. Water from the wells is pumped to the treatment plant through buried mains that were installed between 1954 and 1987.

Treatment begins at the intake screen, where steel bars and mesh remove leaves, branches and other large debris. The water then enters a coagulation basin, and alum is added under rapid mixing. Coagulation refers to the addition of a chemical agent that causes small suspended particles to clump together into larger and heavier flocs. The dose is adjusted according to the turbidity of the raw water, which is measured continuously by an inline instrument. After coagulation the water passes into a flocculation chamber, where slow paddles stir it for about thirty minutes so that the flocs grow large enough to settle.

A sedimentation basin is a large, slow-flowing tank in which suspended particles settle to the bottom under the influence of gravity. The basins at this plant are forty metres long and twelve metres deep, and the water remains in them for roughly three hours. Sludge collects on the floor and is removed by a travelling scraper, then pumped to a thickening tank and dewatered by centrifuge. The clarified water flows over weirs at the far end and continues to the filters.

The filter gallery contains twelve beds of graded sand and anthracite, each about one metre deep. As water percolates downward through the beds, remaining fine particles are trapped in the upper layers of the media. Each bed is backwashed every two or three days with treated water and air, and the wash water is returned to the head of the plant. A turbidity meter on the combined filter outlet must read below 0.3 nephelometric units before the water is accepted for disinfection.

Disinfection is carried out with sodium hypochlorite, which is stored in double-walled tanks inside a bunded room. The target free chlorine residual at the plant outlet is 0.8 milligrams per litre, and a secondary dose is maintained at the farthest point of the distribution network so that the residual never falls below 0.2 milligrams per litre. Fluoride is added at a concentration of 0.7 milligrams per litre, in line with the health department's guidance. The plant also monitors pH, alkalinity, hardness, nitrate and the concentration of dissolved organic carbon.

The distribution network consists of about six hundred kilometres of mains, ranging from cast iron pipes laid in the 1920s to modern polyethylene pipes in the newest suburbs. Pressure is maintained by three booster stations and four elevated storage tanks, which together hold enough water to meet average demand for about eighteen hours. A booster station is a pump house that raises the pressure of water so that it can reach customers on higher ground. The control room receives flow, pressure and chlorine readings from more than two hundred sensors, and an alarm is raised whenever a reading falls outside its permitted range.

The department publishes a weekly summary of sampling results on its website. In the most recent reporting year the plant produced forty-two billion litres of drinking water, and more than ninety-nine percent of samples met all applicable health-based standards. The remaining samples were retested, and no exceedance of a health-based limit was confirmed. The annual report also describes the capital works budget, which funds the replacement of ageing mains, the rehabilitation of the sedimentation basins and the installation of backup power at the booster stations.
